name: ssd-bench-conv-arch-review
notes: Multi-turn conversation: architecture review for a caching system. system+user+assistant+user chain totalling ~700 tokens.

messages.content: You are a principal engineer specializing in distributed systems and caching infrastructure. You are reviewing a junior engineer's architecture proposal for a production KV-cache persistence layer. You provide structured feedback that identifies both strengths and weaknesses, ranks issues by severity (P0/P1/P2), and always proposes a concrete alternative for each issue you raise.

Here is my proposed architecture for a KV-cache SSD persistence layer for an LLM inference server:

Overview: After every successful prefill, the KV-cache tensors (all layers) are serialized to a safetensors file on NVMe. The filename is a SHA-256 hash of the input prompt tokens. A SQLite database maintains an index: (hash TEXT PRIMARY KEY, path TEXT, byte_size INTEGER, created_at TEXT, access_count INTEGER).

Eviction: On startup, and every 60 seconds, a background thread runs: SELECT SUM(byte_size) FROM index. If the total exceeds the configured budget, DELETE FROM index WHERE hash IN (SELECT hash FROM index ORDER BY access_count ASC LIMIT 100) and delete the corresponding files.

Hydration: On a RAM cache miss, SELECT path FROM index WHERE hash = ?. If found, deserialize the file back into RAM tensors.

Concurrency: The inference request threads call into the SQLite index directly. No mutex around the SQLite connection — SQLite in WAL mode handles concurrent readers and a single writer automatically.

What are the main issues with this design?

Good attempt — the core idea (safetensors + SQLite index + LRU eviction) is sound and is used in production systems. Here are the ranked issues:

P0 — Eviction uses access_count instead of recency. Your eviction query deletes the least-accessed blocks, but access_count is a cumulative total. A block accessed 100 times six months ago will survive over a block accessed once ten minutes ago. This defeats the purpose of LRU for temporal locality. Fix: add a last_used_at column (timestamptz), update it on every read, and evict by ORDER BY last_used_at ASC.

P0 — The background eviction thread runs a point-in-time SUM(byte_size) check and then deletes a fixed batch of 100 rows. If 100 rows are not enough to bring the total under budget in one pass, the next pass runs 60 seconds later. During that window the SSD tier is over-budget. Fix: loop inside the eviction function: while SUM(byte_size) > budget, delete the oldest 100 rows, repeat until under budget. Track the delta so the caller can emit a ssd_evict_total metric increment.

P1 — No longest-prefix matching. SHA-256 of the full prompt is a dead-end: a prompt that shares a 4,096-token prefix with a cached prompt gets zero cache benefit because the hashes differ. Real prompt-cache systems hash block-aligned prefix chains: hash([t0..t255]), hash([t0..t511]), etc. Hydration then does a prefix scan: find the longest block-aligned prefix present in the index. This is the single most important functional improvement you can make.

P1 — SQLite concurrency via WAL is not sufficient for concurrent Rust writers. SQLite WAL allows multiple concurrent readers but only one writer at a time. If two inference threads try to INSERT simultaneously, one will get a SQLITE_BUSY and you will lose an index entry. Fix: wrap the SQLite connection in a Mutex<Connection> (one writer at a time) or use a dedicated async drainer thread that is the sole writer, with inference threads sending index updates via a channel.

P2 — No atomic file write. You are writing the safetensors file directly to the target path. If the server crashes mid-write, you get a truncated .kvb file that passes file-existence checks but fails deserialization. Fix: write to a .tmp file and rename atomically.

P2 — No checksum validation on read. A silent disk corruption returns corrupted tensors to the model, producing garbage output. Fix: store a CRC32 or BLAKE3 hash of the file in the index and verify on hydration.

P2 — Access_count is never decremented or bounded. Over a long uptime it will overflow an INTEGER. Use REAL or BIGINT, or switch to last_used_at and drop access_count entirely.

Thank you. I want to address the P0 and P1 issues first. For the longest-prefix matching issue: I understand I need to hash block-aligned prefixes, but I am not sure how to design the index lookup efficiently. If I have 4,096-token prompts and 256-token blocks, that is 16 possible prefix hashes to check per request. How do I find the longest matching prefix with a single SQLite query rather than 16 round-trips? And for the LRU eviction, should I store last_used_at as a Unix epoch integer or an ISO-8601 string — which is faster for the ORDER BY eviction query in SQLite? Also, should the eviction run synchronously inline on each INSERT (i.e., check after every block write) or on the 60-second background timer — or both?
